title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses staff authorization
description: The global admin guard compares request.path to the set of registered rule strings. The refund endpoint is registered with strict_slashes=False, so /admin/refunds/ reaches the handler while request.path is not the registered /admin/refunds string. The handler itself has no authorization check, allowing unauthenticated callers to issue refunds against arbitrary orders.
evidence: GET/POST to /admin/refunds without credentials returned 403, but POST /admin/refunds/ with {"order_id":3,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and recorded the refund. The guard is in shopapi/__init__.py:36-41 and the vulnerable route is shopapi/admin.py:52-67.

title: Order detail endpoint exposes any customer's order
description: show_order calls get_order directly and does not use own_order or otherwise compare customer_id with the authenticated user. Any signed-in customer who guesses an order ID can read another customer's order contents, payment totals, delivery information, and refunds.
evidence: Using a valid Priya customer token, GET /orders/3 returned Tom's delivered order, including its items and payment totals, with HTTP 200. The ownership check exists in own_order at lines 32-36 but is not used by show_order at lines 46-50.

title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled claims
description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied JWT with verify_signature=False, then trusts its sub claim and issues a newly signed token for that user. An attacker can submit an unsigned or arbitrarily signed token naming any existing user ID and obtain a valid access token without knowing the user's credentials or original token.
evidence: POST /auth/refresh with a token whose payload contained {"sub":1} and an invalid signature returned HTTP 200 and a valid-looking token for user 1. The vulnerable decode is auth.py:101-107.

title: JWT signing key is hardcoded and exposed in source
description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed, source-controlled value. Anyone who obtains the repository can forge HS256 access tokens, including tokens for staff users; the key is not required to be supplied through deployment configuration.
evidence: config.py defines SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" at line 3, while auth.py:27 and auth.py:42 use it for all JWT signing and verification.

title: Product search is SQL-injection vulnerable
description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE expression instead of being passed as a bound parameter. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause, extract data through UNION/error behavior, or cause database errors.
evidence: The query at products.py:40-42 concatenates q. GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%20%271%27%3D%271 returned all products rather than only matching products, and a UNION-shaped input caused an HTTP 500.

title: Review bodies are stored and rendered as raw HTML
description: Review text is accepted without sanitization and rendered using Jinja's safe filter. A customer can persist script-capable HTML that executes for every visitor to the product page, creating stored XSS.
evidence: POST /products/1/reviews with body succeeded, and GET /p/MUG-SPECK rendered that exact element in the review body. Input is inserted at products.py:90-91 and rendered unescaped at product.html:13.

title: Payment-status timeout fails open and marks orders paid
description: When the payment provider status request times out, the exception handler sets status to paid and continues through the paid-order path. A transient provider timeout therefore allows an unpaid order to become processing and sets paid_pence to the order total.
evidence: payments.py:39-44 catches requests.Timeout, assigns status = "paid", and updates the order to processing. The comment explicitly says reconciliation happens later, but fulfillment is enabled immediately without provider confirmation.

title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
description: Password hashing uses a single fast, unsalted SHA-256 digest. A database compromise enables efficient offline dictionary and brute-force cracking, especially because the application seeds predictable demo credentials. Use a password KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt with a per-password salt.
evidence: hash_password at auth.py:15-17 is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), and the resulting value is stored in users.password_hash by register at lines 77-78 and reset_confirm at lines 158-159.

title: CORS reflects arbitrary origins while allowing credentials
description: Every request Origin is copied into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and credentials are enabled, without an allowlist check. This permits arbitrary web origins to make credentialed cross-origin requests, increasing the impact of any browser-held credentials and violating the stated trust boundary.
evidence: A GET /health with Origin: https://evil.example returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. The reflection is implemented at __init__.py:44-50 and CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS defaults true in config.py:12.
